nodes.title: Kubernetes Deployment strategies: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A Kubernetes Deployment manages rolling updates and rollbacks for stateless Pods. CKAD exams test strategy types, rollout commands, and how resource limits interact with scheduling.

flashcards.back: RollingUpdate: gradually replaces old Pods with new ones (zero downtime). Recreate: terminates all old Pods before starting new ones (brief downtime).

flashcards.front: maxSurge and maxUnavailable — what do they control?
flashcards.back: maxSurge: how many extra Pods above the desired count can exist during rollout. maxUnavailable: how many Pods can be down at once. Both accept absolute numbers or percentages.

flashcards.front: Command to roll back a Deployment to the previous revision?
flashcards.back: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>  (add --to-revision=N to target a specific revision from rollout history).
Liveness: kills and restarts the container if it fails. Readiness: removes the Pod from Service endpoints if it fails (does not restart).

questions.q: An application runs 5 replicas in a Deployment. During a rolling update, the developer wants at least 4 Pods always running and no more than 7 Pods at any one time. Which settings achieve this?
choices: maxSurge: 7 and maxUnavailable: 4
maxSurge: 2 and maxUnavailable: 1
maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 1
minReadySeconds: 4 and maxSurge: 2
questions.explanation: With 5 replicas, `maxUnavailable: 1` guarantees at least 4 running (5 − 1) and `maxSurge: 2` caps total Pods at 7 (5 + 2). `minReadySeconds` is a delay before a new Pod counts as available — not a Pod-count control. The third option (surge 7, unavailable 4) describes maximums of 12 total and as few as 1 running, far outside the requested envelope. `maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1` keeps total at 5 max — surge is needed to exceed the desired count.

questions.q: A new application version has a problem and the team wants to revert to the previous revision after inspecting history. Which kubectl command sequence performs this?
choices: kubectl rollout status deployment/app then kubectl rollout pause deployment/app
kubectl describe deployment app then kubectl delete deployment app and reapply
kubectl rollout history deployment/app then kubectl rollout undo deployment/app
kubectl get deploy -o yaml then kubectl apply -f previous-version.yaml
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout history` lists the Deployment's revisions and change-causes; `kubectl rollout undo` rolls back to the previous revision (or `--to-revision=N` for a specific one). Deleting and recreating the Deployment causes downtime and loses the controller's revision history. `kubectl rollout pause` halts further rollouts — it does not roll back. Capturing the live YAML and reapplying skips the controller's revision machinery and is fragile: you have no record of the prior ReplicaSet image/template.

questions.q: A developer runs `kubectl rollout status deployment/web` and the command hangs without completing. What is MOST likely happening?
choices: The kubectl command has a bug and needs to be rerun with --force
The Deployment was paused with kubectl rollout pause and is awaiting resume
The Deployment has no rollout in progress so the command should have returned immediately
The rollout is in progress but new Pods are failing their readiness probes
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout status` blocks until the rollout finishes or fails. The textbook reason for it to hang is that the new ReplicaSet's Pods are not becoming Ready — the controller waits for readiness before replacing the next old Pod. Check `kubectl get pods` and `kubectl describe pod` on a new replica for the probe failure. `--force` is not a flag for `rollout status`. If there is no rollout in progress the command exits quickly with `deployment ... successfully rolled out`. A paused rollout is plausible but rarer than failed probes; the question asks for the MOST likely cause.

questions.q: A Deployment named `app` is currently paused (via `kubectl rollout pause`). A developer then updates the image and environment variables. When will these changes take effect?
choices: Immediately — pausing only affects new deployments, not in-place updates
After 5 minutes — the default pause timeout expires automatically
When the Pod restarts due to a liveness-probe failure, which automatically resumes the rollout
Only after `kubectl rollout resume deployment/app` is run; all queued template changes then roll out together
questions.explanation: `rollout pause` stops the Deployment controller from reconciling template changes; you can edit the template repeatedly, and once you run `rollout resume` all accumulated changes ship in a single rolling update. Liveness-probe restarts never resume a paused rollout. There is no automatic pause expiry — pauses are sticky until you resume. Pausing absolutely affects in-place updates; that is the whole point.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: A developer creates a ClusterIP Service named `api-service` in namespace `backend`. A Pod in namespace `frontend` needs to reach it. Which DNS name resolves to this Service from the frontend namespace?
choices: api-service.backend.svc.cluster.local — full FQDN for a Service in the backend namespace
api-service alone — works from any namespace via the cluster search domain
api-service.backend.cluster.local — drop the `svc` segment from the FQDN
backend.api-service.svc.cluster.local — namespace must come first
questions.explanation: Kubernetes DNS follows `<service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`, so `api-service.backend.svc.cluster.local` is correct from any namespace. The first option reverses service and namespace. The second drops the `svc` segment, which is required (Services live under `svc`, Pods under `pod`). The bare name `api-service` only resolves from inside the `backend` namespace because the search domain prepends the caller's namespace.

questions.q: A developer creates a Service of type NodePort for a web application. Which statement CORRECTLY describes how this Service works?
choices: NodePort requires a cloud load balancer to route external traffic to the Pods
NodePort routes traffic only to Pods that happen to run on the node receiving the request
NodePort is identical to ClusterIP and is only reachable from inside the cluster
NodePort exposes the Service on a static port on every node's IP, forwarding to the backing Pods
questions.explanation: NodePort allocates a port (default range 30000–32767) on every node; kube-proxy forwards traffic from `<NodeIP>:<NodePort>` to a backing Pod, regardless of which node the Pod runs on. ClusterIP is internal-only — that is the contrast NodePort exists to bridge. By default kube-proxy load-balances across all Pods cluster-wide (you only get node-local routing if you set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`). LoadBalancer is the type that depends on a cloud LB; NodePort works on its own and is often the building block used under a LoadBalancer.

questions.q: A developer wants to expose an application to other Pods inside the cluster but NOT outside. Which Service type provides internal-only access?
choices: LoadBalancer — with spec.loadBalancerIP set to an internal IP address
ClusterIP — the default Service type, reachable only from within the cluster
ExternalName — resolves the Service name to an internal CNAME
NodePort — restricted to traffic originating from inside the cluster
questions.explanation: ClusterIP allocates a virtual IP from the Service CIDR that only nodes and Pods can route to — no external exposure, and it is the default type. LoadBalancer always asks the cloud for an externally reachable LB (internal-LB annotations exist but are provider-specific and not part of the Service type itself). NodePort opens a port on every node's external IP — by definition externally reachable. ExternalName is a DNS CNAME; it does not produce a cluster IP and usually points OUT of the cluster.

questions.q: A developer needs a Service that maps a cluster-internal DNS name to an external hostname like `database.example.com`. Which Service type provides this?
choices: LoadBalancer Service with externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
ClusterIP Service backed by a manually authored Endpoints object pointing at the external host
ExternalName — creates a DNS CNAME in cluster DNS that resolves to the external hostname
NodePort Service with externalIPs covering each cluster node
questions.explanation: `spec.type: ExternalName` plus `spec.externalName: database.example.com` makes the cluster DNS return a CNAME pointing at the external host — pure DNS aliasing, no proxying. NodePort with externalIPs publishes a Service ON the cluster nodes for external clients; it does not redirect cluster Pods to external hosts. A manual Endpoints object can work for IP targets but does not handle a changing external hostname or do DNS aliasing. LoadBalancer provisions an external IP for inbound traffic; it does not forward outbound from Pods to an external DNS name.

nodes.title: Expose a web app in Kubernetes

data.scenario: Expose a stateless web app to external HTTPS traffic. Order the objects you create.

nodes.explanation: A Deployment manages the pod replicas, a Service gives them one stable virtual IP and load-balances across them, and an Ingress exposes the Service to external HTTP(S) traffic with host/path routing.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A developer creates a Kubernetes Secret to store a database password. Running `kubectl get secret db-secret -o yaml` shows the password as a string of garbled-looking characters. What is the correct explanation?
choices: The password is encrypted with AES-256 and can only be decrypted with the cluster master key
The value is stored as a TLS certificate, which is why it looks like a long random string
The password is hashed with SHA-256 and cannot be recovered from the stored value
The password is Base64-encoded, not encrypted — anyone with read access can decode it
questions.explanation: Secret values are Base64-encoded in the YAML for safe transport of binary bytes — `echo '...' | base64 -d` recovers the original. They are not encrypted by default; real protection comes from RBAC, encryption-at-rest in etcd, or an external secret manager. The Secret here is type `Opaque` (or `generic`), not `kubernetes.io/tls`. Hashing would make the value unrecoverable by the consuming Pod, defeating the purpose. There is no built-in 'cluster master key' AES-256 wrapping unless the operator explicitly enabled encryption-at-rest providers.

questions.q: A developer needs to pass a database password stored in a Kubernetes Secret as an environment variable `DB_PASSWORD` inside a container. Which Pod spec snippet achieves this?
choices: env: [{name: DB_PASSWORD, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-secret, key: password}}}]
env: [{name: DB_PASSWORD, value: my-secret}] — inline the literal Secret name as the env value
volumes: [{secret: {secretName: db-secret, key: password}}]
envFrom: [{secretRef: {name: DB_PASSWORD}}] — inject every key from the Secret named DB_PASSWORD
questions.explanation: `valueFrom.secretKeyRef` pulls a single Secret key into a named environment variable — the precise way to expose one secret as one env var. The volume form (`volumes:`) projects Secret data onto the filesystem, not as env vars (and `key` is not a valid field at that level). `value: my-secret` would set the literal string 'my-secret', not the Secret's contents. `envFrom.secretRef` injects every key from a Secret named `DB_PASSWORD` (clearly not the intent — DB_PASSWORD is the env var name, not the Secret name).

questions.q: A developer needs to create a Kubernetes Secret from a literal value using an imperative command — specifically storing `password=s3cr3t`. Which command is correct?
choices: kubectl create secret generic db-secret --from-file=password=s3cr3t
kubectl create secret docker-registry db-secret --password=s3cr3t
kubectl create secret tls db-secret --cert=s3cr3t
kubectl create secret generic db-secret --from-literal=password=s3cr3t
questions.explanation: `--from-literal=<key>=<value>` is the flag for inline key/value pairs on a `generic` (Opaque) Secret — exactly the case asked. `--from-file=password=s3cr3t` would treat `s3cr3t` as a filename and try to read it; it does not store the literal string. `tls` Secrets require a cert and key file pair, not a literal string. `docker-registry` Secrets carry registry credentials and demand `--docker-server/--docker-username/--docker-email`; `--password` alone is incomplete and the wrong secret type for a generic password.

questions.q: A developer needs to restrict traffic so that only Pods labelled `app=frontend` can reach Pods labelled `app=database`. All other traffic to the database Pods should be blocked. Which resource enforces this?
choices: A ResourceQuota limiting how many connections non-frontend namespaces may open
A ClusterIP Service with session-affinity rules that pin frontend to database
A NetworkPolicy on the database Pods allowing ingress only from app=frontend Pods
An Ingress with a whitelist annotation naming the frontend application Pods
questions.explanation: A NetworkPolicy with `podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: database}}`, `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and `ingress.from.podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: frontend}}` is the canonical pattern; once a NetworkPolicy selects a Pod, all non-matching traffic is denied. Ingress is for L7 HTTP routing into the cluster, not Pod-to-Pod policy. ResourceQuota caps API object counts and aggregate resource usage in a namespace — it does not control L4 connectivity. Service session affinity sticks a client to a backend Pod; it does not gate which clients are allowed.

questions.q: A developer applies a NetworkPolicy with `spec.podSelector: {}` (empty selector) and `policyTypes: [Ingress]` with no `ingress` rules. What effect does this have?
choices: All Pods in the namespace are completely isolated from ingress traffic (default-deny ingress)
Kubernetes rejects the manifest as invalid because no ingress rules are listed
All Pods in the namespace allow all ingress traffic because the selector matches everything
Only Pods without any labels are affected by this policy
questions.explanation: An empty `podSelector` matches every Pod in the namespace; `policyTypes: [Ingress]` with an empty (omitted) `ingress` list means 'apply an ingress policy that allows nothing' — the canonical default-deny pattern. Kubernetes accepts the manifest; an empty ingress list is valid and deliberate. The empty selector matches all Pods regardless of labels. The 'allow all' interpretation reverses the semantics: empty rules deny, not permit.

questions.q: A NetworkPolicy allows egress from Pods labelled `app=worker` to port 5432 (PostgreSQL). The worker Pods still cannot connect to the database. Ingress is unrestricted at the network plugin level. Which additional NetworkPolicy might be blocking the connection?
choices: A cluster-wide NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} denying egress for every selected Pod
A NetworkPolicy on the database Pods restricting ingress to a different set of source labels
A NetworkPolicy on the worker Pods restricting ingress from other workloads
A NetworkPolicy on the database Pods that permits egress to any external endpoint labelled with app=worker
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicies are evaluated on BOTH endpoints — egress must be allowed at the source AND ingress must be allowed at the destination. If the database has an ingress policy that does not list `app=worker` as an allowed source, the connection is dropped on arrival. The first option talks about egress FROM the database — that controls outbound traffic from the DB, not inbound from workers. A default-deny on egress would have blocked the workers entirely (and would contradict the stated 'egress is allowed'). Restricting ingress on the worker Pods affects who can talk TO the workers, not whether workers can reach the DB.

questions.q: A developer needs to run a batch process that completes 10 items in total, running 3 tasks in parallel at any time. Which Job spec fields control this behaviour?
choices: spec.replicas: 10 and spec.maxSurge: 3 (Deployment-style fields)
spec.completions: 3 and spec.parallelism: 10 (total then parallelism)
spec.activeDeadlineSeconds: 10 and spec.backoffLimit: 3 (timeout fields)
spec.completions: 10 and spec.parallelism: 3 (total then parallelism)
questions.explanation: `spec.completions` is the total number of successful Pod completions required (10); `spec.parallelism` caps how many Pods may run concurrently (3). The first option swaps the two values. `replicas`/`maxSurge` are Deployment fields, not valid on Jobs. `activeDeadlineSeconds` is a wall-clock timeout (seconds, not items) and `backoffLimit` is a retry cap after failure — neither controls work distribution.

questions.q: A developer sets `spec.activeDeadlineSeconds: 300` on a Job. What happens if the Job's Pods have not completed within 300 seconds?
choices: Kubernetes moves the Job to a suspended state and terminates its Pods 300 seconds later
Kubernetes terminates all Pods owned by the Job and marks the Job Failed with reason DeadlineExceeded
The Job continues running but Kubernetes records a warning event in the namespace
Kubernetes pauses the Job and waits for manual intervention
questions.explanation: `activeDeadlineSeconds` is a hard wall-clock budget for the entire Job; on expiry the controller deletes the Pods and the Job status reports `Failed` / `DeadlineExceeded`. There is no automatic 'suspend then terminate later' workflow. The Job is not paused awaiting a human — that would be `spec.suspend: true`, which is set, not auto. The Job does not silently continue past the deadline; the deadline is enforced. Contrast `backoffLimit`, which caps retries after individual Pod failures rather than total wall-clock time.
